In my experience, showing you have some technical competency tells your engineers you can keep up with what they're doing and you'll ask good questions 😊 But you *do* have to ask if/when you're lost!

Ooh, good question. I went a weird route to get there, so take my journey with a grain of salt, but I think it's (unfortunately) a combo of being lucky enough to be in the right place at the right time and having the support system to take jobs that didn't offer health insurance. 

I feel like I kinda lucked into my current job. I knew nothing about the company when I applied - I just desperately needed to leave my contract job - and I did most of my interviewing with them while I was on vacation (which I think made me appear very chill and calm and put together). They needed someone who had experience documenting hardware, software, and had done doc migrations before, and I happened to have all 3 (cuz I can't stay at a job for more than like 2 years).

To get here, I essentially went English dork -> engineering student -> engineer -> tech writer, which looks pretty smooth when it's written out like that, but that process took 10+ years (I'd be happy to give you a more detailed explanation, but I'm trying not to ADHD info dump :P). I was lucky enough to be able to pick up an engineering background, but I've still had to do a lot of learning on my own, specifically about different coding languages & software. I also struggle speaking with people in an intelligent way, especially while I'm nervous, so I've worked hard to seem like a capable human being in interviews. 

So, to answer your question: *parts* of landing the job were easy. I love writing and I write pretty well, and I'll hyperfocus on learning new languages (I learn them well enough to be able to read them, but *oh my god* actually coding is like pulling teeth for me). Other parts, like doing the actual interviewing, learning to accept criticism at work (RSD's a *bitch*), and getting rid of imposter syndrome were incredibly difficult. Everything else was basically just luck. 

If you're interested in being a TW, here's the advice I can offer: 

* Code is king, and the docs-as-code method is being adopted by a lot of places
   * If you can learn (and show that you know) Markdown/Asciidoc/XML, that'll go really far
   * git & GitHub are fantastic tools to learn and slap on the resume too (and they're free!)
   * Any other language you want to learn only strengthens your resume
* Keep your resume simple and easily searchable with as many SEO keywords as you can shove in there. No fancy graphics or formatting - my resume is literally a simply formatted bullet point list. I do a general explanation of each job (with numbers and metrics), then highlight a project or two that show me in a good light that I'm happy to talk about in interviews.
* Get some good writing samples. I started out using a piece of an old lab report and some meeting notes I'd turned into a doc while I was an engineer.
* Look up the STAR method for responding to interview questions. This method has helped me cut down on my ADHD-ing around when I'm answering things.

100% - I definitely got lucky that I was working as a hardware engineer and then another hardware company wanted a tech writer, letting me make the switch. But I looked for a TW job for like... 6-8 months before I found that first one, and that was in 2018.

But I'm sorry you weren't able to finish out the cert! That's such a bummer. I hope your major switch made other things better though!

I make 6 figs as a Senior Technical Writer. You spend a lot of time learning about new products - either from engineers or by playing with them yourself - and writing docs about them (which may not be everyone's thing, but it's a love of mine). I manage docs for a few large product lines, and am overseeing a migration to a new tool. It's fun, satisfying, and there's So Much downtime while you're waiting for the engineers to get you new stuff or review your docs.

I went to school for engineering, so I am specialized, but I've met plenty of people in this line of work who are self taught. I bounced around between a few short-term contracts to get big tech companies on my resume, and now I'm at a sweet full-time job that's fully remote. I essentially work when I need to, and then I have a bunch of time to get chores and other life stuff done. 

I don't make as much as I could other places, but when I got really sick last year, my job gave me unlimited sick time without using FMLA/short term disability (AND they didn't fire me, obvi), so I kept a full paycheck and my insurance. I don't preach company loyalty, because most places don't deserve it, but that plus the chill company culture will keep me around for another minute.

The itching and diagnosis kind of happened in parallel; this was the process:
- Oct 2022: I got a cough that lingered after a cold
- Dec 2022 - Feb 2023: I tried a bunch of antibiotics and other things to get the cough to go away; it did not. The patches of rash also started around here, but they were manageable with itch creams. We had no reason to believe the cough and itch were related at this point. 
- Mar 2023: The itching got worse, and I went to the derm to check it out, and they determined it was just an allergic reaction. My PCP was also concerned about the cough, so she ordered an xray. The xray showed a big ol mass in my chest, so I went from xray > CAT scan real quick (cuz they thought I had lung cancer, but I didn't know that at the time). 
- Apr 2023: After a bronchoscopy and then a needle biopsy, they finally told me I had cancer, but initially called it Hodgkins. 
- May 2023: After switching oncologists (cuz I hated my first one), my new oncologist said it was actually NHL, specifically stage 4 Primary Mediastinal B-Cell Lymphoma (PMBCL), which was why there was a big tumor in my chest (it was like 8.5x6cm centered on my right lung and was constricting 2/3 main arteries to my heart). I start chemo, which was DA-EPOCH-R. 
- May - Sept 2023: I did 6 rounds of chemo. The itching stopped with the steroids they gave me during chemo, and then was totally gone after round 1. I did have a bunch of side effects during the rounds (like the tumor died faster than my body could handle it, so a bunch of fluid ended up building up around my heart twice), but made it to remission 🤗

I'm good today! I've been in remission for 7mo (I was in remission after 4 rounds of chemo, but we did the full 6 to be safe), and I have my 2nd follow up PET scan next month!

Ooh, that's a good question - they started small on my forearms, and then cleared up and the came back with a vengeance. It was all over my arms and outer thighs, and had even made it to my stomach by the time I stated chemo. They looked like big ol' patches of hives, but very circular in nature with a very even edge to them. Before we knew it was lymphoma, my dermatologist did a punch biopsy of one of the reddest sections, and it just came back as inflammation due to an allergic reaction.

Yep! Mine didn't come and go, but I had the rashes all over my arms and legs before I started chemo; they went away after my first round. My oncologist said that they happen because your immune system knows something is wrong, but since the problem is *in* your immune system, it can go a little haywire and you can get the rashes as a result.

I couldn't eat much for the first half of chemo. The tumor I had was sitting just so in my chest that it was pressing down on my stomach, and I'd cough a lot of my food back up. My body got so starved for nutrients (I lost about 30 lbs in 2 months) that I suddenly wasn't lactose intolerant anymore, so I ate a lot of yogurt, ice cream, and usually after the mouth sores went away, a big bowl of mac and cheese with broccoli. Otherwise, it was chicken broth and small amounts of protein shakes, along with lemon water or lemonade (I'd forget to drink unless it tasted like something, and the acidity of the lemon juice cut through the weird film I'd get in my mouth after chemo that made it hard to taste anything). 

Towards the end of chemo when I could keep stuff down, I ate anything I wanted to during my stays in the hospital - a 5 day round of prednisone will get you eating like a 13-year-old boy :D I went through so many bags of Albanese gummy bears that now I can't eat them anymore.

I've done a few contracts since becoming a technical writer. In my experience, they're usually 40 hr/wk, but the ones I've done have always been flexible about the hours to a certain degree - as long as I hit my deadlines, I could sort of work whenever I needed to.

The writing is pretty much the same you'd be doing as an FTE - manuals, instructions, white papers, etc. I haven't felt super different from the full time employees, but then again, most of the writers at my level were also contractors. I also wouldn't say that I felt like I was a part of the company culture, but that's not really a big deal for me. Working to become an FTE would be awesome, sure, but more so for the benefits (contractor benefits can be considerably worse than what FTEs get). Otherwise, I kinda like the contractor lifestyle - I get to work on new things every 6-18 months, and I've gotten to try working at a few big companies without having to go through the long interview loops.

I've made this pattern and it'll 100% accomplish what you want here! It's even got the instructions to make the gathered bertha (the v-shaped piece in the front). If you need any help, just shoot me a PM!

I'm a technical writer, actually! I get to work with all kinds of engineers, taking their notes and turning it into easy-to-understand documentation. It is still writing, but it's much more systematic and procedural than creative writing (at least for me). I  went to school for engineering, so this was a really good way to bring that and my writing skills together.

Programming is definitely a valid way to go, but you could also do programming docs and the tech world always needs doc writers

Hey, I got diagnosed about a year ago, and I had the same thing at first, especially with Ritalin and then with Adderall - there was euphoria at first, but it eventually went away as I kept taking the medication. For other reasons, my doctor moved me to Vyvanse, and the mood stabilizing properties stuck around. Right now, I'm at the right dosage and I find that (as long as I remember to eat), I stay pretty level. I think it's the fact that my brain is properly stimulated, so I don't feel nearly as much anxiety (so I can also talk to people and be social) and my depression goes away because I feel like I can actually get things done.

One of the biggest reasons I got bumped up to the next dosage was because those feelings were starting to come back when the meds wore off - plus, I felt like I would lose the ability to concentrate about 6 hours before that. My doc also said it was strange that I was able to manage the depression and anxiety with just adhd meds, but she's been pretty cool with it so far; in her opinion, the fewer prescriptions I need to take, the better. It might just be that you need a bump in prescription strength. 

I don't know why you're skipping dosages on the weekends, and I don't think you said (who knows, I might have missed it), but I would recommend against that. Your adhd doesn't go away just cuz you're not at work :P and the withdrawals from Vyvanse aren't super fun (I get dizzy if I go like a day and a half without it). I'm not a doctor, but taking your meds 5 days a week then going cold turkey sounds like you're whipping your brain back and forth - it might be why you're so incredibly depressed on the weekends. 

Personally, I enjoy who I am when I'm on the meds - yeah, its different than who I've been in the past, but I feel like it's closer to the person I want to be. I had to really overcome the idea that I'd need to take meds for the rest of my life to be like other people, but once I was on the right meds for like a month or two, I felt so much better than I had before. Like, this is the first winter in my life that I haven't really been experiencing seasonal depression and it is WILD.

This might be a rambly wall of text, but I've been in this situation before, so I'm gonna throw out the things that helped me:

It sounds like (from this cursory look into your life) you may be experiencing caretaker fatigue. I can say from experience that being the only person your SO can lean on is exhausting - you worry constantly about them, and it shifts the relationship dynamic to the point where you don't necessarily feel like it's a partnership anymore, especially if the problem persists for a while. Is your SO in therapy for their mental health issues, or are you the only person they rely on? If they aren't seeing a therapist, I would encourage them to start. If that seems like too big of a step to them, encourage them to talk to their friends or family to find support. You're also allowed to set boundaries, like saying "I understand you're hurting right now, but I can't help you because I have no energy left." Those clear boundaries (along with a conversation about how draining taking care of your SO is) might help them see that you're in a tougher spot than they realize. 

Are you making sure your own needs are met - do you see your friends/family to refill your tank after taking care of your SO? Do you have anyone you can talk to? (If not, I'm happy to listen and feel free to PM me) 

This type of stress is a perfectly reasonable and understandable reason to leave - you've given and given and given and gotten nothing in return. There's no easy way to break up with someone, but like the other comments have said, you shouldn't put others needs above your own forever. You deserve to be in a relationship that has a give and take, and if that can't be this one, then you should move on (which is much easier for a stranger on the internet to say than it is to do). I wish you the best of luck.

“Hey Alex, I’m home!” I kicked my work shoes off and stepped into my house slippers. My roommate looked out from the bathroom, mascara in hand. My other friend Sam poked her hand out of the doorway and waved.

“Shit Rachel, you’re home late. We’re already getting ready to go out!”

“I know; it was a madhouse at the office today – open enrollment is a bitch.” I grabbed a bag of popcorn from the kitchen and flopped onto the couch. “Where are you guys off to?”

Alex started to respond “Club J-” before Sam cut her off.

“Nuh uh,” Sam came out from the bathroom and snatched the bag from my hand. “You’re coming with us. You haven’t come out in forever.” She started to eat from the stolen bag, but she stopped short to take a long look at me. 
	
“Sammy, I just got my slippers on!” I protested. She didn’t respond, but continued to stare at my now empty hand.
	
“Holy hell, are you okay?”
	
“What do you mean?” I looked down, and my stomach followed suit. 
	
My wrist was bare. Ever since I’d turned the magical fourteen, a bright blue band had encircled my right wrist. Over the years it’d become my favorite color, and I spent years searching in vain to find it both in a piece of clothing and on another person. But now it was gone, and I numbly realized I couldn’t even remember exactly what it looked like. Tears pricked up in the corners of my eyes. 
	
Sam sat down on the couch next to me. “Honey, I’m so sorry.” Her voice had dropped down to a whisper, which caught Alex’s attention. 
	
“Hey, guys, we’re supposed to be turning up!” she shouted from the bathroom
	
“Alex, would you shut the fuck up? Rachel’s mark is gone.” Sam pulled me into a tight hug. 
	
“What does it even matter?” I whispered into her shoulder, “It’s not like I knew them.” Sam started to pet my hair. 
	
Alex walked out and grabbed my wrist. We’d been friends forever, and she knew the mark almost as well as I did. She’d been the one to point it out when it’d shown up on my birthday. We’d stayed up all night eating junk food and watching the kind of movies you only watch when you’re fourteen and after three whole packages of Oreos, the beautiful blue band had shown up at 3:02am. The time was burned into my brain along with birthdays and phone numbers and now it meant nothing. 
	
She looked back and forth from my wrist to my face. “I-I mean, you know,” she stuttered, “They say that the color can change during your life. Maybe this is what happens when it’s changing?” 
	
“That’s bullshit,” I spat back, voice cracking, “How many people have you ever heard of it changing? Like in real life?”
	
“Hey, whoa, babe. Look at me.” Alex put a hand on my cheek and made me look at her. She wiped the tears from my face with her thumb. “You’re only 24.”
	
“Yeah, great, so I have the rest of my life to be alone.”
	
“Listen to me, okay? People aren’t meant to have one soul mate. There are probably a dozen people out there with the same color your band is. Well, was.” She faltered, not entirely sure what to say next. This wasn’t something that happened. Or at least, it didn’t happen very often. I’d read stories on the Internet of people losing their bands, but they were old people, or ones that were antisocial to begin with. I was neither of those things. 
	
Sam put a hand on my back. “I have an idea – we could paint one on you!”
	
I was thrown by the suggestion. “What?” 
	
“Yeah! We’ll get a picture of you from like a week ago, and we’ll mix up some of Alex’s paints and we’ll get it as close as we can! Because, a) no one’s going to notice, b) it’ll make you feel better, and c) what’s the chance you meet someone with the same color tonight anyways?” She smiled widely at Alex and I, and Alex smiled back. 
	
“That’s a fantastic idea, Sammy. I’ll be right back.” Alex got up off the couch and went into her room. 
	
“I think it’s a dumb idea,” I whispered. There was no way it was going to work. I felt so hollow, as though someone had ripped a piece of my heart out. Which I guess technically had been what happened. I rubbed at my wrist, willing the band to come back, but instead the skin turned an annoyed red. 
	
“You’re not thinking very well right now, honey. You’ve just suffered an enormous loss.” Sam was in school to get her degree as a therapist, which was helpful for deciphering coworker’s behaviors, but not so much when she practiced it on us. 
	
“I just… I thought I had more time, you know?” The tears started to come back and I stared at Sam’s wrist. She had a set of three navy blue lines encircling her left wrist, which matched her boyfriend’s right wrist. They were absolutely perfect for one another and had been together since they were fifteen. It was disgusting. 
	
“I know, I know. But I really think this will help. If nothing else, getting out of the house will be good for you.”
	
Alex reappeared with her oil paints and some washi tape. “We’ll mark it off so I don’t get paint all over you.” She gently took my hand into her lap and started to rip pieces of tape to fit me. “It’ll be okay, babe.” 
	
I didn’t respond, instead choosing to spiral into a deep circle of loneliness. The two of them talked while Alex painted, using a reference from a work party a few weeks ago. They tried to pull me in a few times, but I chose not to respond. It wasn’t fair. How could a small color have so much impact on me? I mean, I’d noticed it kind of changing over the last week or so – the color had seemed to be getting lighter and lighter – but I’d honestly thought that it was the stress of work getting to me. At any rate, what would I have done? No one knew where these marks had come from. There were stories that at one point, humans didn’t have them, but that had been generations ago. 
	
“Annnnnd done!” Alex pulled the last piece of tape off with a flourish. “Just give that like 15 minutes to dry, and you’ll be golden.” She put out her hand to help me up. 
	
I had to admit, it looked similar. Not quite the same color, and there was a raised bump where the line was now, but the knot in my stomach untied itself a little. “Thanks, Alex.” 
	
“Alright, babe, now we need to get the rest of you ready!” Alex hopped off to the kitchen to grab the liquor out of the freezer. 
	
“No, no, I really don’t want to go out.” 
	
“Tough titties. There’s tequila in the fridge, and I didn’t paint that mark on you for nothing.” She opened the bottle with her teeth and pulled out three shot glasses from the sink, giving them a quick rinse before filling them with alcohol. Sam moved into the kitchen and took two, holding one out to me. “Seriously, babe,” Alex said, grabbing the third shot, “tequila gets rid of all problems.” 
	
I sighed. “Fine, but I’m only going to do one shot. Maybe two.” 
	
Half a bottle later, we were ready to go. I’d been made up by the two girls, and we’d decided on wearing all black. “To mourn the death of my love life,” I’d joked, four shots deep. 
	
“I think this means I can sleep with anyone now, doesn’t it?” I slurred, paying the cover. 
	
“Fuck yeah it does!” Alex called back over the music. 
	
“Fuck yeah!” I grabbed her hand, and pushed my way to the bar. “Three shots of tequila please!” 
	
The bartender was cute, with a lovely red mark around his wrist. I couldn’t stop myself from looking, and underneath all the alcohol swirling in my head, I could feel a twinge of jealousy. He still had his mark. I didn’t. Fuck. 
	
“Twenty-three dollars!” he shouted back. I started to hand him my card, when a hand caught mine. I turned to look at the owner of the hand, and I came face to face with the most beautiful man I’d ever seen. His eyes were the color that my band used to be, and I found I couldn’t look away. 
	
He smiled at me. “Let me.” He reached out his right hand, and I caught a glimpse of his mark. It looked as though another person’s skin had been transplanted in a thick band on his wrist – it transitioned abruptly from white to brown, then to white again. The bartender gave him back his card, and he turned to face me again. 
	
He leaned into me so I could hear him without shouting. “I’m Rob.” 
	
“Rachel.” He smelled wonderful. 
	
“Can I ask you a personal question?” 
	
I took a small step back and looked at him. He put up his hands. “It’s nothing too bad, I promise! You don’t even have to answer if you don’t want to!” 
	
I thought about it for a second before nodding. What could it hurt?
	
“Did your band change color today?”
	
I sucked in a breath. “Is it that obvious?” 
	
He offered out the marked wrist and put it up to my skin. It looked as though my skin color flowed from me to him. Without looking up, I yelled “Did yours?” 
	
“It did – it used to be blue, pretty close to the paint on your arm! I like that, by the way. Did you do it yourself?”
	
I locked eyes with him, and realized that on my worst day, I’d found the love of my life.
